- If sentiment shows strong bullish (≥0.5) or bearish (≤-1) momentum in recent days, model should adjust forecast slope to match sentiment direction, especially if price is trending sharply.
- When model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows sharp downward correction (e.g., >10% drop from forecast peak), reduce forecast slope or add early reversal buffer.
- If model overestimates price after a recent spike (e.g., forecast >75% above recent high), apply downward bias correction, especially if sentiment is neutral or slightly bearish.
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative sentiment (e.g., multiple -1.00 entries), model should not assume continuation of upward trend; apply mean reversion bias toward recent 5-10 day average.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >15% from model in first 5-7 days, adjust forecast to reflect early volatility or sentiment-driven correction.
- If sentiment is bullish but true outcome is consistently below forecast, consider lagged effect — model may be overreacting to sentiment; reduce forecast slope or add smoothing factor.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows strong upward momentum (e.g., >5% daily gain), consider sentiment-driven momentum bias — increase forecast slope if sentiment is positive.
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed, model should avoid over-optimistic forecasts; use recent 7-day average as baseline for correction.
